description_full: Loma Negra Compañía Industrial Argentina Sociedad Anónima, together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and sells cement and its derivatives in Argentina. It operates through Cement, Masonry Cement, and Lime; Concrete; Railroad; Aggregates; and Others segments. The company offers masonry cement, aggregates, ready-mix concrete, concrete, and lime to wholesale distributors, concrete producers, industrial customers, and others. It also provides rail transportation services; and treats and recycles industrial waste for use as fuel and raw material. It markets its products under the Loma Negra, Plasticor, Cacique Max, Loma Negra Plus, and Lomax brands. Loma Negra Compañía Industrial Argentina Sociedad Anónima was incorporated in 1926 and is based in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Loma Negra Compañía Industrial Argentina Sociedad Anónima operates as a subsidiary of Intercement Trading E Inversiones Argentina Sociedad Limitada.

financial_summary: Loma Negra Compania Industrial  is a small-cap basic materials business with a $1.0B market cap on $768M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding. Operating margins are expanding by +3.0pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $57M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.81× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.0×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.
